rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Some commentators say Moses completed the full ten-year term and then stayed for another ten years.
rows.anchor: Some say that Moses completed the term of the entire ten years and then stayed ten more (Q, R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Moses seeing the fire also appears at 20:9, 26:10, and 27:7.
rows.anchor: The incident of Moses seeing the fire is also mentioned in 20:9; 26:10; 27:7.

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: A firebrand is a burning log or branch used to start another fire.
rows.anchor: A firebrand refers to a burning log or branch with which one might start another fire (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Most scholars
rows.claim: Most scholars consider al-ʿAnkabūt a Makkan sūrah.
rows.anchor: scholars maintain that al-ʿAnkabūt is a Makkan sūrah

rows.speaker: many scholars
rows.claim: Many who consider the sūrah Makkan hold that its first ten verses were revealed in Madinah.
rows.anchor: many of those say the first ten verses were revealed in Madinah (Āl, IJ, Q, Tb)

rows.speaker: a minority
rows.claim: A minority considers the sūrah Madinan.
rows.anchor: A minority maintain that it is Madinan (IJ)

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: Some say the first ten verses were the last verses revealed in Makkah.
rows.anchor: some say that the first ten verses were the last verses revealed in Makkah (Āl, IJ)

rows.speaker: several sources, including ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: The Prophet recited Sūrahs 29 and 30 together in prayer, sometimes followed by Sūrah 36.
rows.anchor: among them the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah, the Prophet would recite Sūrah s 29 and 30 together in his prayers, sometimes followed by Sūrah 36.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from the spider’s house, a metaphor for the frailty of this world.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the useof the spider’s house as a metaphor for the frailty of this world in v. 41:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spider parable evokes human ignorance of God and the Hereafter: taking other protectors is a fragile position that leaves people unprepared for life after death.
rows.anchor: This verse evokes the central theme of this sūrah, that human beings are not aware of the true nature of God and the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening challenges believers who think faith alone will spare them life’s trials; it calls for continued striving, since truth rarely prevails without effort and sacrifice.
rows.anchor: Al-ʿAnkabūt begins by challenging the believers who think that their faith or belief alone will save them from the trials of this life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah gives examples of earlier communities whose people disobeyed the messengers sent to them.
rows.anchor: examples of previous communities, such as those of the prophets Noah, Abraham, Ḥūd, and Ṣāliḥ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This section discusses the Qur’an’s purifying efficacy and reaffirms its transcendent Source.
rows.anchor: After discussing the Quran and its purifying efficacy, while reaffirming its transcendent Source (vv. 44–51)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah responds to disbelievers’ objections and addresses the nature of their beliefs.
rows.anchor: the sūrah responds to the objections posed by the disbelievers and addresses the nature of their beliefs (vv. 52–63)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion reflects on this world’s ephemerality and assures believers that thankfulness and striving for God lead to guidance.
rows.anchor: It concludes with a meditation on the ephemerality of this world, assuring those who believe in God and the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This frequently quoted verse parallels 3:185 and 21:35.
rows.anchor: Cf. 3:185; 21:35. In the immediate context

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because death is inevitable, the previous verse’s command to worship God means everyone must prepare for death through worship.
rows.anchor: In the immediate context, this frequently quoted verse explains why the previous verse enjoins worship of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After returning to God, each soul learns its place in the Hereafter; believers receive lofty Garden abodes, elsewhere described as abodes above abodes.
rows.anchor: After souls have returned to God, each is informed of its place in the Hereafter. Believers are given lofty abodes of the Garden, which are elsewhere described as lofty abodes above which are lofty abodes (39:20).

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the Garden’s transparent rooms are prepared for those who feed others, speak well, pray and fast continually, and pray at night while others sleep.
rows.anchor: Regarding them the Prophet is reported to have said, “In the Garden there are rooms whose outside can be seen from the inside

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise to settle believers alludes to the hardship of emigration and assures those who leave things for God of lofty abodes in the Hereafter, if not in this life.
rows.anchor: That God shall settle them alludes to the difficulties some may confront in emigrating, addressed in v. 56

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unlike disbelievers who demand the punishment be hastened, believers patiently endure the present and trust God for what He will provide in the future.
rows.anchor: such individuals are patient with what confronts them in the present and trust in their Lord regarding what He will provide them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise’s truth echoes 30:6 and is cross-referenced with 4:122, 10:4 and 10:55, 18:21, 28:13, 31:33, 35:5, 40:55 and 40:77, 45:32, and 46:17.
rows.anchor: That God’s Promise is indeed true (cf. 4:122; 10:4, 55; 18:21

rows.speaker: IJ, Ṭ, Z
rows.claim: One interpretation is that God promises to aid the Prophet and make him prevail.
rows.anchor: Here it is understood as a reference to God’s Promise to aid the Prophet, to make him prevail (IJ, Ṭ, Z)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that God promises to make the Prophet’s veracity clear.
rows.anchor: and to render his veracity clear (R).

rows.speaker: IJ, Q
rows.claim: The warning about disbelievers’ uncertainty can mean they must not make one restive about one’s religion.
rows.anchor: not let them make one restive regarding one’s own religion (IJ, Q).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Though grammatically addressed to one person, the command is understood as addressing the Prophet’s community as a whole.
rows.anchor: it is understood as having been addressed to the Prophet’s community as a whole (Q)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb yastakhiff, translated as disquiet, can mean inducing levity or rushing someone so that they become unsteady.
rows.anchor: Disquiet translates yastakhiff, which can also mean to induce another to levity or to force another to do something in a hurry and so become unsteady.

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A further interpretation is that the verb means making someone heedless or ignorant, leading them into error and transgression.
rows.anchor: It is also understood to mean making another heedless or ignorant, so that the person then falls into error and transgression (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Luqmān is generally considered a Makkan sūrah revealed just after al-Rūm.
rows.anchor: is believed to have been revealed during the Makkan period immediately after the previous sūrah, al-Rūm

rows.speaker: some scholars
rows.claim: Some hold that verses 27–29 were revealed in Madinah.
rows.anchor: some maintain that vv. 27–29, perhaps the most frequently cited verses of the sūrah, were revealed during the Madinan period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah is named for Luqmān, described as a sage or prophet who gives wisdom to his son.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the mention of the sage or prophet Luqmān (vv. 12–13), who conveys wisdom to his son

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening follows from the previous sūrah: steadfast adherence to the Wise Book and its guidance prevents disquiet, while idle discourse brings it.
rows.anchor: being steadfast in adhering to the Wise Book (v. 2) and following its guidance are what prevent one from being disquieted, while following idle discourse (v. 6) will lead to disquiet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 7’s image of disbelievers turning away from God’s signs as if deaf echoes 30:52, that the Prophet cannot make the deaf hear.
rows.anchor: The observation in v. 7 that the disbelievers turn away from God’s signs as if they do not hear also echoes the assertion in 30:52

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah focuses on worship, obedience, and gratitude; Luqmān teaches God’s greatness and oneness and worship of Him alone, linked to obedience and gratitude to parents unless they oppose allegiance to God.
rows.anchor: The focus of this sūrah is upon worship, obedience, and gratitude. Luqmān enjoins his son to recognize the Greatness of God, His Oneness, and the need to worship only Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The teaching balances support for the community and family loyalty with the primacy of one’s relationship with God.
rows.anchor: people should support the community and maintain familial allegiances, but not to the detriment of their relationship with God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes by warning that neither parent nor child can help the other on Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: The sūrah closes with a warning that neither parent nor child can help one another on the Day of Judgment (v. 33).
